BERT4Rec’s masked-item objective prevents bidirectional target leakage; diagnostics must retain the appended prediction mask and exclude the target from visible history. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690) provides the architectural basis. [CAPE, WWW 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09027) emphasizes that attention relies on positional encoding to represent order, motivating separate checks of item content and position. Neither establishes that perturbation sensitivity reveals causal user intent.

Suggested controlled protocol, synthesized from these mechanisms: freeze each user’s candidate set and trained network; compare deletion of k recent versus k oldest interactions against repeated random k-deletions. Report paired changes in target score, candidate-relative margin, rank and validation HR@10, with uncertainty. Compare compacted deletion with position-preserving masking; deletion otherwise changes content, length and positions together. Add replacements matched on training-item frequency and available title/description similarity, plus shuffles that preserve the item multiset and prediction-mask position. Keep left padding and readout correct. Differences across controls indicate model sensitivity to recency, context or positional representation; they do not establish preference mechanisms. Masking itself changes the input distribution, so agreement across intervention types matters.

Attribution reliability requires more than plausible heatmaps. [Adebayo et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03292) motivate parameter-randomization checks; [Hedström et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.02383) identify noise and similarity-metric pitfalls. Adapt these as temporary diagnostic randomizations of the same network, without fitting additional predictors. Compare attribution-guided deletion against random deletion, repeat perturbation draws, inspect signed effects and baseline sensitivity. Passing these checks supports faithfulness to this network, not causal explanations of users.
